data.title: TD Synnex to acquire specialty distributor BlueStar
data.description:
TD Synnex, one of the world’s largest technology distributors, announced that it signed a definitive agreement to acquire Clearwater, Florida-based BlueStar.

BlueStar is a specialty distributor of barcode scanners, point-of-sale systems, RFID, robotics and other business technology. The deal, which still needs regulatory approval, gives TD Synnex deeper domain knowledge in a niche corner of IT distribution. Both companies say they will keep operating independently until it closes.

What acquiring BlueStar means for TD Synnex

TD Synnex’s leadership expressed enthusiasm for the BlueStar deal.

“BlueStar has built an outstanding reputation through specialization, technical expertise and an unwavering commitment to its partners,” said Reyna Thompson, president of North America for TD Synnex, in a release announcing the deal. “We’re excited about the opportunity to combine BlueStar’s expertise in AIDC, operational technology, mobility, RFID, point-of-sale and related technologies with the global resources, investments and reach of TD Synnex.”

In addition, TD Synnex lauded the new expertise that BlueStar will infuse into the combined company.

“In addition to BlueStar’s portfolio, the specialized knowledge and expertise within its team are central to the differentiated support and services it provides,” said Miriam Murphy, president of EMEA for TD Synnex. “Combined with the global capabilities of TD Synnex, those strengths have the potential to enhance opportunities for customers and vendors of both companies.”

Implications for BlueStar’s business

Industry observers assessed that the deal could be a mixed bag for the smaller vendors and resellers that relied on BlueStar.

Mike Danford, a branding and marketing expert and owner and chief revenue officer of marketing agency Adverio, called the deal a specialty shelf getting absorbed into a general store.

“Smaller vendors who sold through BlueStar can gain reach, but they risk losing the category buyer who actually knew their products,” Danford said.

Danford added that a vendor that was a big fish in a small pond now becomes a small fish in a much bigger pond, with more reach and less of the distributor’s attention.

“It’s the same squeeze smaller brands face on the big marketplaces,” Danford said.

Nevertheless, he added that there could be an upside, too.

“We constantly see that a truly great offer, priced reasonably for its category, can grow far faster once it gains visibility on a bigger network than it could in a smaller marketplace with fewer buyers,” he explained. “For standout brands, a larger buyer pool can be the break they need.”

The deal could offer more products and better support, but also raise concerns about pricing, fewer supplier choices, and losing personalized service.

“Early on, customers tend to gain a broader catalog and more resources. The cost tends to land later on the smaller vendors, who go from a curated lineup to one of many lines at a distributor serving 150,000 customers, with fewer distributors to play against each other on terms,” Danford said.

BlueStar’s technology sales

Technology advisers who work with smaller providers saw a similar trade-off.

Tom Cloud, founder of CIO Advisory, works with private-equity investors and middle-market companies on technology diligence, IT strategy and post-close execution. He said smaller technology providers could view the acquisition in different ways.

“The upside is scale,” he said, echoing Danford’s comments. “A larger distributor can potentially give smaller VARs and MSPs access to more product lines, better logistics, broader financing options and more resources than a specialty distributor could provide on its own.”

Meanwhile, he said, the risk is losing what made the distributor valuable in the first place.

“Smaller providers often rely on distributor relationships for more than just fulfillment,” Cloud stated. “They depend on product expertise, responsive support, credit flexibility and people who understand a particular niche.”

Cloud said if those relationships become more centralized or standardized after the acquisition, smaller partners may feel the impact quickly.

Moreover, Cloud noted that from an operator standpoint, he would be watching three things closely: whether credit and purchasing terms change, whether the specialized support remains intact, and whether smaller partners continue to get the same level of attention after integration.

“I would also treat this as a vendor-concentration issue,” he said. “If a provider has become heavily dependent on one distributor for certain product categories, an acquisition is a good time to review alternative sources and make sure the business is not exposed to a single point of failure, which a lot are.”

data.title: Amazon Prime Big Deal Days in October drove $9.86 billion in online spending, Adobe says
data.description:
Amazon Prime Big Deal Days returned on Oct. 6 and 7 in 2026, and data published by Adobe shows that shoppers spent more than when the event was held on Oct. 7 and 8 in 2025.

The two-day sales event, which fell on a Tuesday and Wednesday in both years, saw online shoppers spend $9.86 billion at U.S. retailers in its latest iteration, according to Adobe analysts. Adobe’s data is based on direct transactions online, including more than 1 trillion visits to U.S. retail sites, 100 million SKUs and 18 product categories, according to the company.

More than 200 of the Top 2000 largest online retailers used Adobe for web analytics in 2025. They combined for more than $836 billion in ecommerce sales that year.

Amazon ranks No. 1 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 2000 Database. The database is how Digital Commerce 360 tracks the largest North American online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

Amazon is also No. 3 in Digital Commerce 360’s Global Online Marketplaces Database. That database ranks the 100 largest such marketplaces by third-party gross merchandise value (GMV).

How much did consumers spend during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days in October?

Online sales at U.S. retailers increased 8.5% year over year while Amazon Prime Big Deal Days was going on in 2026. As the total, $9.86 billion, grew, so did the rate of increase. In 2025, sales were up 7.3% to reach $9.09 billion.

Adobe sees this activity leading retailers to invest in earlier pre-holiday promotions than they would otherwise hold.

Those discounts reached a peak of 20% off listed price, according to Adobe. As they did, the deepest discounts appeared in merchandise categories including computers, televisions, electronics, toys and apparel.

Among these categories, electronics sales spiked, up by 85% from average sales levels in September 2026, Adobe assessed. Meanwhile, toy sales increased by 158%, and video game sales were up 90%. Sales in the personal care products category were up 73% from September.

In electronics specifically, sales of products such as headphones and speakers were up 300% from September, with smartwatch sales up 255%, camera sales up 135% and smartphone sales up 130%. In the meantime, ahead of Halloween, costume sales increased by 610% and candy sales grew by 180%, Adobe reported.

How shoppers made purchases during Prime Big Deal Days in October

Adobe also tracked how online shoppers made purchases over the two-day sales period, noting that purchases made on mobile devices made up 52.0% of all online sales, roughly $5.1 billion and up 12.8% year over year.

In many cases, buy now, pay later (BNPL) services saw heavy use as well. Adobe credited BNPL with enabling 6.0% of online orders over the two days, giving those options a role in $692.3 million in sales. That total was up 4.0% from October’s Prime event 2025.

Looking ahead, Adobe projects that BNPL will drive more than $1 billion in spending on Cyber Monday, which falls on Nov. 30 in 2026.

data.title: Albertsons expands OpenAI work, adding enterprise ChatGPT use
data.description:
Albertsons Companies continues to explore how artificial intelligence (AI) best fits into its operations and ecommerce strategy, which now includes an expanded enterprise partnership with OpenAI and a ChatGPT plugin for the Safeway banner.

OpenAI detailed the companies’ latest work in a blog post on Oct. 1, noting that Albertsons’ teams were using ChatGPT to “navigate complexity, accelerate workflows and move promising ideas toward production faster.”

Albertsons is No. 17 in the Top 1000 Database. That database ranks the largest online retailers in North America by annual ecommerce sales.

OpenAI described the scope of its work with Albertsons as including ChatGPT Enterprise, in addition to what it referred to as “custom AI-powered experiences for its customers, data-driven recommendations and promotional insights built with the OpenAI API.”

Albertsons’ portfolio included more than 2,200 stores across its banners. Those banners encompass its namesake stores, Safeway, Vons, Jewel-Osco, Shaw’s, ACME and Tom Thumb.

Albertsons rolled out its Safeway plugin for ChatGPT in August.

“Research tells us that consumers are increasingly interested in using AI to help with grocery shopping,” said Jill Pavlovich, senior vice president, digital customer experience at Albertsons Companies, at the time. “By enabling our plugin in ChatGPT, we are making grocery shopping as simple as having a conversation by meeting our customers when and how they choose to shop.”

The plugin operates within the ChatGPT app experience. Once connected to ChatGPT and a shopper’s Safeway account, it enables a chat-style interface for planning grocery lists and making purchases.

Albertsons’ recent history of AI use

Previously, Albertsons became one of the first retailers to test ChatGPT’s ads in 2026. OpenAI welcomed the grocer, along with Target and Williams-Sonoma in the pilot, and its ads have continued to evolve alongside ChatGPT’s agentic commerce strategy throughout the year.

In addition to OpenAI, Albertsons has also worked with Google on an AI assistant experience. Notably, Albertsons was the first retailer to use Google Cloud’s conversational AI solution in 2025.

Looking ahead, OpenAI expects Albertsons to leverage its large language model to create internal predictive models, along with recommendations and insights about the grocer’s activities, thanks to employee tools, commerce-related apps and advertising solutions that OpenAI will power there.

data.title: Walmart opens automation-infused fulfillment center in California
data.description:
Walmart announced the opening of its fifth next-generation fulfillment center in Stockton, California. The facility, spread across 900,000 square feet, will increase Walmart’s storage capacity and allow it to fulfill more orders across California and the West Coast, according to the retailer.

Walmart ranks No. 2 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database, which tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

Walmart is also No. 37 in Digital Commerce 360’s AI Commerce Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

What distinguishes Walmart’s new fulfillment center in Stockton

The centerpiece of Walmart’s Stockton fulfillment center is its automated, high-density storage and retrieval system that brings products directly to associates rather than requiring workers to travel the facility floor. That reduces an otherwise 12-step fulfilment process to just five steps, leaving more time for workers to focus on higher-value tasks, Walmart said.

Walmart now processes more than half of its ecommerce fulfillment volume through automated facilities, according to figures the company shared with investors along with Walmart online sales updates in its fiscal Q2 earnings results. 3,100 of Walmart’s U.S. stores also use automated freight to some capacity. 

Combined with Walmart’s broader fulfillment network, the company says its next-generation fulfillment centers now enable it to reach 95% of the U.S. population with next- or two-day shipping.

“We’re bringing together associates with advanced technology and automation to create a safer, more efficient operation that can fulfill more orders and get products to customers faster,” said Karisa Sprague, senior vice president in fulfillment operations at Walmart U.S. in a written statement. “This facility is an important investment in the Central Valley and a critical part of how we’re building the next generation of Walmart’s fulfillment network across the West Coast.”

Fast delivery’s importance for Walmart

Delivery speed has been central to Walmart’s ecommerce plan in recent quarters.

Walmart U.S. online sales grew 26% in Q1, with delivery speed cited as “a key catalyst for growth around the world” by Rainey. Walmart can now reach about 60% of the U.S. population through delivery in 30 minutes or less, a capability it has expanded to 38 U.S. markets.

Meanwhile, store-fulfilled delivery has more than doubled over the past two years, with more than 36% of those orders delivered in under three hours. 

“Speed matters, and we have a significant competitive advantage,” Walmart CEO and president John Furner told investors in August.

How Walmart Fulfillment Services will use the center

Importantly, the Stockton facility is not only for Walmart’s first-party ecommerce business. 

Walmart Fulfillment Services (WFS), the company’s end-to-end third-party fulfillment offering for marketplace sellers, will also use the space to fulfill orders for merchants selling on Walmart.com. That makes the opening directly relevant for the growing base of brands and distributors selling through the Walmart Marketplace.

Units shipped same day or next day through WFS grew nearly 150% in fiscal Q1, according to John David Rainey, chief financial officer at Walmart.

data.title: Target kicks off holiday season with interactive toy catalog and digital wish lists
data.description:
Target started a major holiday season push on Monday with its new interactive Holiday Kids Catalog, presenting toys in colorful, interactive contexts. The retailer positioned the release as a discovery tool including video content, wish lists and a feature that converts handwritten wish lists into digital shopping lists.

The catalog is available on Target.com and in the retailer’s app. It features nearly 500 toys, games and gifts. However, it is distinct from Target’s separate, curated toy list.

Target is No. 5 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database, which ranks North America’s largest online retailers by annual ecommerce sales.

Target is also No. 54 in Digital Commerce 360’s AI Commerce Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

What’s new in Target’s toy catalog experience

The catalog is designed to function like a shoppable content platform rather than a product grid, according to Target. Shoppers can watch toy demonstrations and video reviews and add items directly to a cart or save them to a wish list. Wish lists can be shared with family members and gift-givers.

In addition, Target implemented a list scanner feature, which allows shoppers who receive or create a handwritten wish list from the printed catalog to scan it in the Target app and convert it into a digital list. Each page of the physical catalog also carries a unique QR code that links directly to the corresponding page in the digital version.

“This year’s digital experience helps families discover toys together, create and share wish lists and find gifts they’ll be excited about all season long,” said Cassandra Jones, senior vice president, Fun101, Target.

Target’s competition with Amazon

Amazon launched its own Holiday Kids Gift Book on the same day as Target’s announcement on Oct. 5.  Now in its ninth year, Amazon’s version features more than 600 toys and gifts, an original illustrated story and family activity pages. 

While Target’s experience is app-native and built around social sharing and creator content, Amazon’s selling point is Alexa integration. Families can unlock a choose-your-own-adventure audio experience through a partnership with Readyland, with kids interacting with the book’s Forest Friends characters via any Alexa-enabled device.

Amazon’s book also comes with its own curated list of top toys chosen by an in-house team of toy experts alongside AI shopping tools. Alexa for Shopping lets parents make requests like “holiday gifts for my 10-year-old daughter” and receive personalized recommendations based on follow-up questions about interests and hobbies. Amazon Lens allows shoppers to scan a product spotted in person or on social media and find it immediately on Amazon.

Amazon ranks No. 1 in the Top 1000 database.

The state of ecommerce at Target

Target’s online sales grew 8.7% year over year in its fiscal Q2 2026, outpacing total comparable sales growth of 3.8%. Same-day delivery drove more than 25% growth in the quarter, and Target fulfilled about 30% more same- and next-day units year over year.

Total net sales in Q2 increased 5.3% to $26.7 billion, though the quarter’s results were boosted by nearly $1 billion in tariff refunds that Target recorded as a reduction to cost of sales. 

The company’s Fun101 category, which covers toys, sporting goods and entertainment, reported double-digit comparable sales growth in Q2, making it the strongest-performing category of the quarter.
